case_info.scenario: A man in his 40s with a history of a matched, sibling allogeneic stem cell transplant for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma 7 years prior presented with a generalized eruption 1 week after receiving a measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccination. The diffuse rash started as pink patches on the face (Figure 1A) and spread to the trunk and extremities within 4 days. Within a day of the MMR vaccination, he reported fever, chills, malaise, myalgias, loose stools, and dyspnea 7 days before the rash began. Pertinent negatives included no itch or pain associated with the rash and lack of any sclerotic skin changes.1He had received a COVID-19 vaccine (Moderna) 2 months prior, and along with MMR, an adjuvanted recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) 1 week prior. Following the patient’s stem cell transplant, he had relapsed disease 1 year later and was treated with donor lymphocyte infusion. Graft-vs-host disease (GVHD) complication of the mouth, eyes, liver, and lungs was treated with systemic steroids and tapered off. The most recent GVHD flare occurred 1 year prior to presentation, and the patient had not been undergoing immunosuppression for 6 months. The patient had also been treated intermittently in the past with oral minocycline for rosacea. Physical examination revealed an erythematous exanthematous eruption with generalized distribution across the trunk, extremities, and face with erythematous erosions noted in the buccal mucosa of the oral cavity. Skin biopsies were performed from the upper right side of the back and right temple (Figure 1B). Further diagnostic testing involved chest radiograph and laboratory tests including complete blood cell count, comprehensive metabolic panel, ferritin, lactate dehydrogenase, and an infectious workup.
case_info.caption: A, Exanthematous eruption of pink papules on the patient’s face. Similar presentation seen distributed generally across the trunk and extremities. B, Hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×400. Folliculosebaceous epithelium depicting scattered dyskeratotic keratinocytes and rare syncytial-type multinucleated epithelial cells (arrowhead).
case_info.explanation: Histopathology demonstrated overlapping features of cutaneous GVHD and cutaneous manifestations of measles. Within the interfollicular and follicular epidermis, there was basovacuolar change with scattered dyskeratotic keratinocytes and satellite cell necrosis, most consistent with either GVHD or measles. Within the folliculosebaceous epithelium (Figure 1B), rare syncytial-type multinucleated cells were seen, also consistent with measles infection.2,3Nasopharyngeal and urine polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was positive for measles. IgM enzyme immunoassay results were positive and IgG enzyme immunoassay results were equivocal. Laboratory results showed complete blood cell count within normal limits and elevated creatinine, aspartate transaminase, alanine transaminase, ferritin, and lactate dehydrogenase levels. Chest radiography portrayed perihilar fullness only. The infectious workup showed positive results for SARS-CoV-2 IgG and IgA receptor-binding domain. The patient’s eruption and symptoms resolved with supportive care alone, without any immunosuppression. No contacts developed any symptoms. Measles is a contagious, airborne viral disease typically presenting with an exanthem after systemic and respiratory symptoms, eg, fever, myalgias, and cough.2,4It is preventable through a 2-dose MMR vaccine series.2,4Adverse events are generally mild with rare serious effects typically in immunocompromised patients.4Within known cases of vaccine-associated measles, presentation includes an acute, generalized eruption, without known distinctive clinical features to distinguish from wild-type measles, which can be differentiated with genotype and PCR. Vaccine-associated measles is exceedingly rare; in cases identified thus far,4there are no known reports of viral transmission. This patient had a history of GVHD and presented with a diffuse rash and systemic symptoms. GVHD management typically involves immunosuppression slowly tapered as tolerated.5During the tapering process, patients may experience GVHD flares,6which may include skin manifestations. Common cutaneous manifestations of chronic GVHD include poikilodermatous, lichenoid, and sclerotic features.7Other common features of GVHD, not sufficient for diagnosis, include erythema, pruritus, and a maculopapular rash involving areas such as ears, face, palms, and soles. After transplant, acute GVHD eruptions may prove difficult to distinguish from viral infections, which can mimic GVHD clinically and may present with interface dermatitis histopathologically (Figure 2). In this case, erythema and a facial maculopapular rash were observed, but this was not definitive for a GVHD diagnosis. Given this case’s systemic symptoms and cutaneous involvement, it proved challenging to completely exclude a concomitant GVHD flare. PCR test positivity for measles 2 weeks after MMR vaccination and resolution without intervention strongly support measles infection. Although the patient had a history of rosacea, pathology and clinical context did not support that diagnosis. An allergic reaction to MMR was not likely given the positive PCR and biopsy results. We suggest that this case represents a rare case of vaccine-induced measles. As typical GVHD management causes immunosuppression, careful consideration must be taken when administering vaccinations. Current recommendations are to continue with nonlive vaccinations such as influenza, especially given the potential of serious infections with immunosuppression.8However, vaccinations may be postponed based on immunosuppression dosage administered, timeline of treatment, and current status of GVHD.5Current recommendations are to avoid live-attenuated vaccines in patients with active GVHD.9In this case, current recommendations would point toward postponing vaccinations, especially live-attenuating, until control of chronic GVHD has been maintained without immunosuppression for a significant duration, even more than 2 years.10

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 0.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Histopathology demonstrated overlapping features of cutaneous GVHD and cutaneous manifestations of measles. Within the interfollicular and follicular epidermis, there was basovacuolar change with scattered dyskeratotic keratinocytes and satellite cell necrosis, most consistent with either GVHD or measles. Within the folliculosebaceous epithelium (Figure 1B), rare syncytial-type multinucleated cells were seen, also consistent with measles infection.2,3Nasopharyngeal and urine polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was positive for measles. IgM enzyme immunoassay results were positive and IgG enzyme immunoassay results were equivocal. Laboratory results showed complete blood cell count within normal limits and elevated creatinine, aspartate transaminase, alanine transaminase, ferritin, and lactate dehydrogenase levels. Chest radiography portrayed perihilar fullness only. The infectious workup showed positive results for SARS-CoV-2 IgG and IgA receptor-binding domain. The patient’s eruption and symptoms resolved with supportive care alone, without any immunosuppression. No contacts developed any symptoms. Measles is a contagious, airborne viral disease typically presenting with an exanthem after systemic and respiratory symptoms, eg, fever, myalgias, and cough.2,4It is preventable through a 2-dose MMR vaccine series.2,4Adverse events are generally mild with rare serious effects typically in immunocompromised patients.4Within known cases of vaccine-associated measles, presentation includes an acute, generalized eruption, without known distinctive clinical features to distinguish from wild-type measles, which can be differentiated with genotype and PCR. Vaccine-associated measles is exceedingly rare; in cases identified thus far,4there are no known reports of viral transmission. This patient had a history of GVHD and presented with a diffuse rash and systemic symptoms. GVHD management typically involves immunosuppression slowly tapered as tolerated.5During the tapering process, patients may experience GVHD flares,6which may include skin manifestations. Common cutaneous manifestations of chronic GVHD include poikilodermatous, lichenoid, and sclerotic features.7Other common features of GVHD, not sufficient for diagnosis, include erythema, pruritus, and a maculopapular rash involving areas such as ears, face, palms, and soles. After transplant, acute GVHD eruptions may prove difficult to distinguish from viral infections, which can mimic GVHD clinically and may present with interface dermatitis histopathologically (Figure 2). In this case, erythema and a facial maculopapular rash were observed, but this was not definitive for a GVHD diagnosis. Given this case’s systemic symptoms and cutaneous involvement, it proved challenging to completely exclude a concomitant GVHD flare. PCR test positivity for measles 2 weeks after MMR vaccination and resolution without intervention strongly support measles infection. Although the patient had a history of rosacea, pathology and clinical context did not support that diagnosis. An allergic reaction to MMR was not likely given the positive PCR and biopsy results. We suggest that this case represents a rare case of vaccine-induced measles. As typical GVHD management causes immunosuppression, careful consideration must be taken when administering vaccinations. Current recommendations are to continue with nonlive vaccinations such as influenza, especially given the potential of serious infections with immunosuppression.8However, vaccinations may be postponed based on immunosuppression dosage administered, timeline of treatment, and current status of GVHD.5Current recommendations are to avoid live-attenuated vaccines in patients with active GVHD.9In this case, current recommendations would point toward postponing vaccinations, especially live-attenuating, until control of chronic GVHD has been maintained without immunosuppression for a significant duration, even more than 2 years.10

Graft-vs-host disease (GVHD) complication of the mouth, eyes, liver, and lungs was treated with systemic steroids and tapered off. [NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.

case_info.explanation: Histopathology demonstrated overlapping features of cutaneous GVHD and cutaneous manifestations of measles. Within the interfollicular and follicular epidermis, there was basovacuolar change with scattered dyskeratotic keratinocytes and satellite cell necrosis, most consistent with either GVHD or measles. Within the folliculosebaceous epithelium (Figure 1B), rare syncytial-type multinucleated cells were seen, also consistent with measles infection.2,3Nasopharyngeal and urine polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was positive for measles. IgM enzyme immunoassay results were positive and IgG enzyme immunoassay results were equivocal. Laboratory results showed complete blood cell count within normal limits and elevated creatinine, aspartate transaminase, alanine transaminase, ferritin, and lactate dehydrogenase levels. Chest radiography portrayed perihilar fullness only. The infectious workup showed positive results for SARS-CoV-2 IgG and IgA receptor-binding domain. The patient’s eruption and symptoms resolved with supportive care alone, without any immunosuppression. No contacts developed any symptoms. Measles is a contagious, airborne viral disease typically presenting with an exanthem after systemic and respiratory symptoms, eg, fever, myalgias, and cough.2,4It is preventable through a 2-dose MMR vaccine series.2,4Adverse events are generally mild with rare serious effects typically in immunocompromised patients.4Within known cases of vaccine-associated measles, presentation includes an acute, generalized eruption, without known distinctive clinical features to distinguish from wild-type measles, which can be differentiated with genotype and PCR. Vaccine-associated measles is exceedingly rare; in cases identified thus far,4there are no known reports of viral transmission. This patient had a history of GVHD and presented with a diffuse rash and systemic symptoms. GVHD management typically involves immunosuppression slowly tapered as tolerated.5During the tapering process, patients may experience GVHD flares,6which may include skin manifestations. Common cutaneous manifestations of chronic GVHD include poikilodermatous, lichenoid, and sclerotic features.7Other common features of GVHD, not sufficient for diagnosis, include erythema, pruritus, and a maculopapular rash involving areas such as ears, face, palms, and soles. After transplant, acute GVHD eruptions may prove difficult to distinguish from viral infections, which can mimic GVHD clinically and may present with interface dermatitis histopathologically (Figure 2). In this case, erythema and a facial maculopapular rash were observed, but this was not definitive for a GVHD diagnosis. Given this case’s systemic symptoms and cutaneous involvement, it proved challenging to completely exclude a concomitant GVHD flare. PCR test positivity for measles 2 weeks after MMR vaccination and resolution without intervention strongly support measles infection. Although the patient had a history of rosacea, pathology and clinical context did not support that diagnosis. An allergic reaction to MMR was not likely given the positive PCR and biopsy results. We suggest that this case represents a rare case of vaccine-induced measles. As typical GVHD management causes immunosuppression, careful consideration must be taken when administering vaccinations. Current recommendations are to continue with nonlive vaccinations such as influenza, especially given the potential of serious infections with immunosuppression.8However, vaccinations may be postponed based on immunosuppression dosage administered, timeline of treatment, and current status of GVHD.5Current recommendations are to avoid live-attenuated vaccines in patients with active GVHD.9In this case, current recommendations would point toward postponing vaccinations, especially live-attenuating, until control of chronic GVHD has been maintained without immunosuppression for a significant duration, even more than 2 years.10

case_info.explanation: Histopathology demonstrated overlapping features of cutaneous GVHD and cutaneous manifestations of measles. Within the interfollicular and follicular epidermis, there was basovacuolar change with scattered dyskeratotic keratinocytes and satellite cell necrosis, most consistent with either GVHD or measles. Within the folliculosebaceous epithelium (Figure 1B), rare syncytial-type multinucleated cells were seen, also consistent with measles infection.2,3Nasopharyngeal and urine polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was positive for measles. IgM enzyme immunoassay results were positive and IgG enzyme immunoassay results were equivocal. Laboratory results showed complete blood cell count within normal limits and elevated creatinine, aspartate transaminase, alanine transaminase, ferritin, and lactate dehydrogenase levels. Chest radiography portrayed perihilar fullness only. The infectious workup showed positive results for SARS-CoV-2 IgG and IgA receptor-binding domain. The patient’s eruption and symptoms resolved with supportive care alone, without any immunosuppression. No contacts developed any symptoms. Measles is a contagious, airborne viral disease typically presenting with an exanthem after systemic and respiratory symptoms, eg, fever, myalgias, and cough.2,4It is preventable through a 2-dose MMR vaccine series.2,4Adverse events are generally mild with rare serious effects typically in immunocompromised patients.4Within known cases of vaccine-associated measles, presentation includes an acute, generalized eruption, without known distinctive clinical features to distinguish from wild-type measles, which can be differentiated with genotype and PCR. Vaccine-associated measles is exceedingly rare; in cases identified thus far,4there are no known reports of viral transmission. This patient had a history of GVHD and presented with a diffuse rash and systemic symptoms. GVHD management typically involves immunosuppression slowly tapered as tolerated.5During the tapering process, patients may experience GVHD flares,6which may include skin manifestations. Common cutaneous manifestations of chronic GVHD include poikilodermatous, lichenoid, and sclerotic features.7Other common features of GVHD, not sufficient for diagnosis, include erythema, pruritus, and a maculopapular rash involving areas such as ears, face, palms, and soles. After transplant, acute GVHD eruptions may prove difficult to distinguish from viral infections, which can mimic GVHD clinically and may present with interface dermatitis histopathologically (Figure 2). In this case, erythema and a facial maculopapular rash were observed, but this was not definitive for a GVHD diagnosis. Given this case’s systemic symptoms and cutaneous involvement, it proved challenging to completely exclude a concomitant GVHD flare. PCR test positivity for measles 2 weeks after MMR vaccination and resolution without intervention strongly support measles infection. Although the patient had a history of rosacea, pathology and clinical context did not support that diagnosis. An allergic reaction to MMR was not likely given the positive PCR and biopsy results. We suggest that this case represents a rare case of vaccine-induced measles. As typical GVHD management causes immunosuppression, careful consideration must be taken when administering vaccinations. Current recommendations are to continue with nonlive vaccinations such as influenza, especially given the potential of serious infections with immunosuppression.8However, vaccinations may be postponed based on immunosuppression dosage administered, timeline of treatment, and current status of GVHD.5Current recommendations are to avoid live-attenuated vaccines in patients with active GVHD.9In this case, current recommendations would point toward postponing vaccinations, especially live-attenuating, until control of chronic GVHD has been maintained without immunosuppression for a significant duration, even more than 2 years.10

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.

[Case]
A man in his 40s with a history of a matched, sibling allogeneic stem cell transplant for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma 7 years prior presented with a generalized eruption 1 week after receiving a measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccination. The diffuse rash started as pink patches on the face (Figure 1A) and spread to the trunk and extremities within 4 days. Within a day of the MMR vaccination, he reported fever, chills, malaise, myalgias, loose stools, and dyspnea 7 days before the rash began. Following the patient’s stem cell transplant, he had relapsed disease 1 year later and was treated with donor lymphocyte infusion. Graft-vs-host disease (GVHD) complication of the mouth, eyes, liver, and lungs was treated with systemic steroids and tapered off. The most recent GVHD flare occurred 1 year prior to presentation, and the patient had not been undergoing immunosuppression for 6 months. The patient had also been treated intermittently in the past with oral minocycline for rosacea. Physical examination revealed an erythematous exanthematous eruption with generalized distribution across the trunk, extremities, and face with erythematous erosions noted in the buccal mucosa of the oral cavity. Skin biopsies were performed from the upper right side of the back and right temple (Figure 1B). Further diagnostic testing involved chest radiograph and laboratory tests including complete blood cell count, comprehensive metabolic panel, ferritin, lactate dehydrogenase, and an infectious workup.

The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Histopathology demonstrated overlapping features of cutaneous GVHD and cutaneous manifestations of measles. Within the interfollicular and follicular epidermis, there was basovacuolar change with scattered dyskeratotic keratinocytes and satellite cell necrosis, most consistent with either GVHD or measles. Within the folliculosebaceous epithelium (Figure 1B), rare syncytial-type multinucleated cells were seen, also consistent with measles infection.2,3Nasopharyngeal and urine polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was positive for measles. IgM enzyme immunoassay results were positive and IgG enzyme immunoassay results were equivocal. Laboratory results showed complete blood cell count within normal limits and elevated creatinine, aspartate transaminase, alanine transaminase, ferritin, and lactate dehydrogenase levels. Chest radiography portrayed perihilar fullness only. The infectious workup showed positive results for SARS-CoV-2 IgG and IgA receptor-binding domain. The patient’s eruption and symptoms resolved with supportive care alone, without any immunosuppression. No contacts developed any symptoms. Measles is a contagious, airborne viral disease typically presenting with an exanthem after systemic and respiratory symptoms, eg, fever, myalgias, and cough.2,4It is preventable through a 2-dose MMR vaccine series.2,4Adverse events are generally mild with rare serious effects typically in immunocompromised patients.4Within known cases of vaccine-associated measles, presentation includes an acute, generalized eruption, without known distinctive clinical features to distinguish from wild-type measles, which can be differentiated with genotype and PCR. Vaccine-associated measles is exceedingly rare; in cases identified thus far,4there are no known reports of viral transmission. This patient had a history of GVHD and presented with a diffuse rash and systemic symptoms. GVHD management typically involves immunosuppression slowly tapered as tolerated.5During the tapering process, patients may experience GVHD flares,6which may include skin manifestations. Common cutaneous manifestations of chronic GVHD include poikilodermatous, lichenoid, and sclerotic features.7Other common features of GVHD, not sufficient for diagnosis, include erythema, pruritus, and a maculopapular rash involving areas such as ears, face, palms, and soles. After transplant, acute GVHD eruptions may prove difficult to distinguish from viral infections, which can mimic GVHD clinically and may present with interface dermatitis histopathologically (Figure 2). In this case, erythema and a facial maculopapular rash were observed, but this was not definitive for a GVHD diagnosis. Given this case’s systemic symptoms and cutaneous involvement, it proved challenging to completely exclude a concomitant GVHD flare. PCR test positivity for measles 2 weeks after MMR vaccination and resolution without intervention strongly support measles infection. Although the patient had a history of rosacea, pathology and clinical context did not support that diagnosis. An allergic reaction to MMR was not likely given the positive PCR and biopsy results. We suggest that this case represents a rare case of vaccine-induced measles. As typical GVHD management causes immunosuppression, careful consideration must be taken when administering vaccinations. Current recommendations are to continue with nonlive vaccinations such as influenza, especially given the potential of serious infections with immunosuppression.8However, vaccinations may be postponed based on immunosuppression dosage administered, timeline of treatment, and current status of GVHD.5Current recommendations are to avoid live-attenuated vaccines in patients with active GVHD.9In this case, current recommendations would point toward postponing vaccinations, especially live-attenuating, until control of chronic GVHD has been maintained without immunosuppression for a significant duration, even more than 2 years.10

case_info.scenario: A man in his 40s with a history of a matched, sibling allogeneic stem cell transplant for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma 7 years prior presented with a generalized eruption 1 week after receiving a measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccination. The diffuse rash started as pink patches on the face (Figure 1A) and spread to the trunk and extremities within 4 days. Within a day of the MMR vaccination, he reported fever, chills, malaise, myalgias, loose stools, and dyspnea 7 days before the rash began. Pertinent negatives included no itch or pain associated with the rash and lack of any sclerotic skin changes.1He had received a COVID-19 vaccine (Moderna) 2 months prior, and along with MMR, an adjuvanted recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) 1 week prior. Following the patient’s stem cell transplant, he had relapsed disease 1 year later and was treated with donor lymphocyte infusion. Graft-vs-host disease (GVHD) complication of the mouth, eyes, liver, and lungs was treated with systemic steroids and tapered off. The most recent GVHD flare occurred 1 year prior to presentation, and the patient had not been undergoing immunosuppression for 6 months. The patient had also been treated intermittently in the past with oral minocycline for rosacea. Physical examination revealed an erythematous exanthematous eruption with generalized distribution across the trunk, extremities, and face with erythematous erosions noted in the buccal mucosa of the oral cavity. Skin biopsies were performed from the upper right side of the back and right temple (Figure 1B). Further diagnostic testing involved chest radiograph and laboratory tests including complete blood cell count, comprehensive metabolic panel, ferritin, lactate dehydrogenase, and an infectious workup.
case_info.caption: A, Exanthematous eruption of pink papules on the patient’s face. Similar presentation seen distributed generally across the trunk and extremities. B, Hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×400. Folliculosebaceous epithelium depicting scattered dyskeratotic keratinocytes and rare syncytial-type multinucleated epithelial cells (arrowhead).
case_info.explanation: Histopathology demonstrated overlapping features of cutaneous GVHD and cutaneous manifestations of measles. Within the interfollicular and follicular epidermis, there was basovacuolar change with scattered dyskeratotic keratinocytes and satellite cell necrosis, most consistent with either GVHD or measles. Within the folliculosebaceous epithelium (Figure 1B), rare syncytial-type multinucleated cells were seen, also consistent with measles infection.2,3Nasopharyngeal and urine polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was positive for measles. IgM enzyme immunoassay results were positive and IgG enzyme immunoassay results were equivocal. Laboratory results showed complete blood cell count within normal limits and elevated creatinine, aspartate transaminase, alanine transaminase, ferritin, and lactate dehydrogenase levels. Chest radiography portrayed perihilar fullness only. The infectious workup showed positive results for SARS-CoV-2 IgG and IgA receptor-binding domain. The patient’s eruption and symptoms resolved with supportive care alone, without any immunosuppression. No contacts developed any symptoms. Measles is a contagious, airborne viral disease typically presenting with an exanthem after systemic and respiratory symptoms, eg, fever, myalgias, and cough.2,4It is preventable through a 2-dose MMR vaccine series.2,4Adverse events are generally mild with rare serious effects typically in immunocompromised patients.4Within known cases of vaccine-associated measles, presentation includes an acute, generalized eruption, without known distinctive clinical features to distinguish from wild-type measles, which can be differentiated with genotype and PCR. Vaccine-associated measles is exceedingly rare; in cases identified thus far,4there are no known reports of viral transmission. This patient had a history of GVHD and presented with a diffuse rash and systemic symptoms. GVHD management typically involves immunosuppression slowly tapered as tolerated.5During the tapering process, patients may experience GVHD flares,6which may include skin manifestations. Common cutaneous manifestations of chronic GVHD include poikilodermatous, lichenoid, and sclerotic features.7Other common features of GVHD, not sufficient for diagnosis, include erythema, pruritus, and a maculopapular rash involving areas such as ears, face, palms, and soles. After transplant, acute GVHD eruptions may prove difficult to distinguish from viral infections, which can mimic GVHD clinically and may present with interface dermatitis histopathologically (Figure 2). In this case, erythema and a facial maculopapular rash were observed, but this was not definitive for a GVHD diagnosis. Given this case’s systemic symptoms and cutaneous involvement, it proved challenging to completely exclude a concomitant GVHD flare. PCR test positivity for measles 2 weeks after MMR vaccination and resolution without intervention strongly support measles infection. Although the patient had a history of rosacea, pathology and clinical context did not support that diagnosis. An allergic reaction to MMR was not likely given the positive PCR and biopsy results. We suggest that this case represents a rare case of vaccine-induced measles. As typical GVHD management causes immunosuppression, careful consideration must be taken when administering vaccinations. Current recommendations are to continue with nonlive vaccinations such as influenza, especially given the potential of serious infections with immunosuppression.8However, vaccinations may be postponed based on immunosuppression dosage administered, timeline of treatment, and current status of GVHD.5Current recommendations are to avoid live-attenuated vaccines in patients with active GVHD.9In this case, current recommendations would point toward postponing vaccinations, especially live-attenuating, until control of chronic GVHD has been maintained without immunosuppression for a significant duration, even more than 2 years.10

case_info.explanation: Histopathology demonstrated overlapping features of cutaneous GVHD and cutaneous manifestations of measles. Within the interfollicular and follicular epidermis, there was basovacuolar change with scattered dyskeratotic keratinocytes and satellite cell necrosis, most consistent with either GVHD or measles. Within the folliculosebaceous epithelium (Figure 1B), rare syncytial-type multinucleated cells were seen, also consistent with measles infection.2,3Nasopharyngeal and urine polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was positive for measles. IgM enzyme immunoassay results were positive and IgG enzyme immunoassay results were equivocal. Laboratory results showed complete blood cell count within normal limits and elevated creatinine, aspartate transaminase, alanine transaminase, ferritin, and lactate dehydrogenase levels. Chest radiography portrayed perihilar fullness only. The infectious workup showed positive results for SARS-CoV-2 IgG and IgA receptor-binding domain. The patient’s eruption and symptoms resolved with supportive care alone, without any immunosuppression. No contacts developed any symptoms. Measles is a contagious, airborne viral disease typically presenting with an exanthem after systemic and respiratory symptoms, eg, fever, myalgias, and cough.2,4It is preventable through a 2-dose MMR vaccine series.2,4Adverse events are generally mild with rare serious effects typically in immunocompromised patients.4Within known cases of vaccine-associated measles, presentation includes an acute, generalized eruption, without known distinctive clinical features to distinguish from wild-type measles, which can be differentiated with genotype and PCR. Vaccine-associated measles is exceedingly rare; in cases identified thus far,4there are no known reports of viral transmission. This patient had a history of GVHD and presented with a diffuse rash and systemic symptoms. GVHD management typically involves immunosuppression slowly tapered as tolerated.5During the tapering process, patients may experience GVHD flares,6which may include skin manifestations. Common cutaneous manifestations of chronic GVHD include poikilodermatous, lichenoid, and sclerotic features.7Other common features of GVHD, not sufficient for diagnosis, include erythema, pruritus, and a maculopapular rash involving areas such as ears, face, palms, and soles. After transplant, acute GVHD eruptions may prove difficult to distinguish from viral infections, which can mimic GVHD clinically and may present with interface dermatitis histopathologically (Figure 2). In this case, erythema and a facial maculopapular rash were observed, but this was not definitive for a GVHD diagnosis. Given this case’s systemic symptoms and cutaneous involvement, it proved challenging to completely exclude a concomitant GVHD flare. PCR test positivity for measles 2 weeks after MMR vaccination and resolution without intervention strongly support measles infection. Although the patient had a history of rosacea, pathology and clinical context did not support that diagnosis. An allergic reaction to MMR was not likely given the positive PCR and biopsy results. We suggest that this case represents a rare case of vaccine-induced measles. As typical GVHD management causes immunosuppression, careful consideration must be taken when administering vaccinations. Current recommendations are to continue with nonlive vaccinations such as influenza, especially given the potential of serious infections with immunosuppression.8However, vaccinations may be postponed based on immunosuppression dosage administered, timeline of treatment, and current status of GVHD.5Current recommendations are to avoid live-attenuated vaccines in patients with active GVHD.9In this case, current recommendations would point toward postponing vaccinations, especially live-attenuating, until control of chronic GVHD has been maintained without immunosuppression for a significant duration, even more than 2 years.10

You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A man in his 40s with a history of a matched, sibling allogeneic stem cell transplant for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma 7 years prior presented with a generalized eruption 1 week after receiving a measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccination. The diffuse rash started as pink patches on the face (Figure 1A) and spread to the trunk and extremities within 4 days. Within a day of the MMR vaccination, he reported fever, chills, malaise, myalgias, loose stools, and dyspnea 7 days before the rash began. Following the patient’s stem cell transplant, he had relapsed disease 1 year later and was treated with donor lymphocyte infusion. Graft-vs-host disease (GVHD) complication of the mouth, eyes, liver, and lungs was treated with systemic steroids and tapered off. The most recent GVHD flare occurred 1 year prior to presentation, and the patient had not been undergoing immunosuppression for 6 months. The patient had also been treated intermittently in the past with oral minocycline for rosacea. Physical examination revealed an erythematous exanthematous eruption with generalized distribution across the trunk, extremities, and face with erythematous erosions noted in the buccal mucosa of the oral cavity. Skin biopsies were performed from the upper right side of the back and right temple (Figure 1B). Further diagnostic testing involved chest radiograph and laboratory tests including complete blood cell count, comprehensive metabolic panel, ferritin, lactate dehydrogenase, and an infectious workup.

[Role]
You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are
about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just

workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or
  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.
- Partial updates are possible: a well-structured point may narrow your uncertainty
  without fully changing your conclusion.
- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge
  when a point has merit even if you do not fully concede.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 10.3. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.caption: A, Exanthematous eruption of pink papules on the patient’s face. Similar presentation seen distributed generally across the trunk and extremities. case_info.explanation: Histopathology demonstrated overlapping features of cutaneous GVHD and cutaneous manifestations of measles. Within the interfollicular and follicular epidermis, there was basovacuolar change with scattered dyskeratotic keratinocytes and satellite cell necrosis, most consistent with either GVHD or measles. Within the folliculosebaceous epithelium (Figure 1B), rare syncytial-type multinucleated cells were seen, also consistent with measles infection.2,3Nasopharyngeal and urine polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was positive for measles. IgM enzyme immunoassay results were positive and IgG enzyme immunoassay results were equivocal. Laboratory results showed complete blood cell count within normal limits and elevated creatinine, aspartate transaminase, alanine transaminase, ferritin, and lactate dehydrogenase levels. Chest radiography portrayed perihilar fullness only. The infectious workup showed positive results for SARS-CoV-2 IgG and IgA receptor-binding domain. The patient’s eruption and symptoms resolved with supportive care alone, without any immunosuppression. No contacts developed any symptoms. Measles is a contagious, airborne viral disease typically presenting with an exanthem after systemic and respiratory symptoms, eg, fever, myalgias, and cough.2,4It is preventable through a 2-dose MMR vaccine series.2,4Adverse events are generally mild with rare serious effects typically in immunocompromised patients.4Within known cases of vaccine-associated measles, presentation includes an acute, generalized eruption, without known distinctive clinical features to distinguish from wild-type measles, which can be differentiated with genotype and PCR. Vaccine-associated measles is exceedingly rare; in cases identified thus far,4there are no known reports of viral transmission. This patient had a history of GVHD and presented with a diffuse rash and systemic symptoms. GVHD management typically involves immunosuppression slowly tapered as tolerated.5During the tapering process, patients may experience GVHD flares,6which may include skin manifestations. Common cutaneous manifestations of chronic GVHD include poikilodermatous, lichenoid, and sclerotic features.7Other common features of GVHD, not sufficient for diagnosis, include erythema, pruritus, and a maculopapular rash involving areas such as ears, face, palms, and soles. After transplant, acute GVHD eruptions may prove difficult to distinguish from viral infections, which can mimic GVHD clinically and may present with interface dermatitis histopathologically (Figure 2). In this case, erythema and a facial maculopapular rash were observed, but this was not definitive for a GVHD diagnosis. Given this case’s systemic symptoms and cutaneous involvement, it proved challenging to completely exclude a concomitant GVHD flare. PCR test positivity for measles 2 weeks after MMR vaccination and resolution without intervention strongly support measles infection. Although the patient had a history of rosacea, pathology and clinical context did not support that diagnosis. An allergic reaction to MMR was not likely given the positive PCR and biopsy results. We suggest that this case represents a rare case of vaccine-induced measles. As typical GVHD management causes immunosuppression, careful consideration must be taken when administering vaccinations. Current recommendations are to continue with nonlive vaccinations such as influenza, especially given the potential of serious infections with immunosuppression.8However, vaccinations may be postponed based on immunosuppression dosage administered, timeline of treatment, and current status of GVHD.5Current recommendations are to avoid live-attenuated vaccines in patients with active GVHD.9In this case, current recommendations would point toward postponing vaccinations, especially live-attenuating, until control of chronic GVHD has been maintained without immunosuppression for a significant duration, even more than 2 years.10

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A man in his 40s with a history of a matched, sibling allogeneic stem cell transplant for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma 7 years prior presented with a generalized eruption 1 week after receiving a measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccination. The diffuse rash started as pink patches on the face (Figure 1A) and spread to the trunk and extremities within 4 days. Within a day of the MMR vaccination, he reported fever, chills, malaise, myalgias, loose stools, and dyspnea 7 days before the rash began. Pertinent negatives included no itch or pain associated with the rash and lack of any sclerotic skin changes.1He had received a COVID-19 vaccine (Moderna) 2 months prior, and along with MMR, an adjuvanted recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) 1 week prior. Following the patient’s stem cell transplant, he had relapsed disease 1 year later and was treated with donor lymphocyte infusion. Graft-vs-host disease (GVHD) complication of the mouth, eyes, liver, and lungs was treated with systemic steroids and tapered off. The most recent GVHD flare occurred 1 year prior to presentation, and the patient had not been undergoing immunosuppression for 6 months. The patient had also been treated intermittently in the past with oral minocycline for rosacea. Physical examination revealed an erythematous exanthematous eruption with generalized distribution across the trunk, extremities, and face with erythematous erosions noted in the buccal mucosa of the oral cavity. Skin biopsies were performed from the upper right side of the back and right temple (Figure 1B). Further diagnostic testing involved chest radiograph and laboratory tests including complete blood cell count, comprehensive metabolic panel, ferritin, lactate dehydrogenase, and an infectious workup.
